name: Japanese bush warbler-brown
lede: Japanese bush warbler-brown is a darker, browner variant of [[japanese-bush-warbler]], and the single most common named color in our painting archive after indigo tea.

sections.title: In Japan: Uguisucha
sections.body:
The name is written 鶯茶, romanized Uguisucha, built from the same bush-warbler word (*uguisu*) as [[japanese-bush-warbler]], with the tea/brown-family kanji 茶 (*cha*) swapped in for *iro*, darkening and browning the parent shade [1]. Our library lists it explicitly as a family variant of the warbler color, not a separate bird or a separate name [1].

The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[autumn]], almost the same shade; [[ivory-brown]] sits close by, darker [2]. [[japanese-bush-warbler]] itself is the next nearest, lighter and yellower [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for Japanese bush warbler-brown in 6,556 of 23,781 paintings, about 27.6 percent, more common than 99 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1600s, in 1,454 of 6,394 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 40 percent of its appearances [3].

The painter most devoted to it is Paul de Vos, in 10 of his 17 paintings here, 2.0 times his peers' rate, as photographed [3]. The earliest archive match is dated 799; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the colors we call Dusty Hazel and Buffy Citrine [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [3].
